sections.html:
About 1,884 square miles lie south and east of Portland in Clackamas County, with Oregon City as the seat and Lake Oswego as the biggest city. The land climbs from river-level suburbs to Mount Hood, so a Lake Oswego house, an Oregon City house and a cabin on the Mount Hood side sit in different markets and under different mixes of taxing districts, yet all of them appear on one county tax roll.

The 2020 Census counted 421,401 residents, the third-highest total in Oregon. Assessed value reached about $66.1 billion in fiscal year 2024-25. Old plats and long-held family parcels are common, so inherited houses with unclear paperwork turn up more often than you might expect.

sections.h2: Wet weather and what it does to houses
sections.html:
Oregon City gets 48.40 inches of precipitation a year. Houses here tend to show the same wear points: moss and worn granules on roofs, clogged gutters, wet crawl spaces with failing vapor barriers, decks, fences and siding that rot at the ground line, and trees that overhang the roof or lean toward the structure.

A house with several of these problems can be hard to list the usual way. Plenty of owners skip the repair bills and sell the house as it is.

sections.h2: Clackamas County tax figures and contacts
sections.html:
Taxing districts imposed about $1.17 billion in property tax for fiscal year 2024-25 on $66.15 billion of assessed value. The average rate was $17.68 per $1,000 of assessed value, and the Measure 5 rate was $9.82 per $1,000 of Measure 5 value. What you pay turns on the specific districts at your address.

OfficeAddress and contact
Assessment and Taxation150 Beavercreek Road, Room 135, Oregon City; 503-655-8671; propertytaxinfo@clackamas.us
HoursOpen Monday through Thursday, 8 a.m. until 4 p.m.
County Clerk (appeal petitions)503-655-8662

sections.h2: Why your bill does not follow the sale price
sections.html:
Tax is figured on the smaller of a home's real market value and its maximum assessed value, so a rising market does not by itself push a bill up. Under Measure 50, every property's 1997-98 assessed value was set back to 90% of its 1995-96 figure, and yearly growth after that stops at 3%.

The cap has exceptions for new construction, remodeling, new subdivisions and rezoning. A buyer who adds square footage can see assessed value jump on that portion.

Measure 5 runs on a separate track. It limits education taxes to $5 and general government taxes to $10 per $1,000 of real market value. Anything above the limit is compressed, with local option levies cut first. A lower market value lowers taxes only if it falls below assessed value, so many owners see no change after a successful appeal.

You can pay by mail, online, through bank bill pay, in person at Room 135 in Oregon City, or in the drop box at the front of the building. Make checks out to Clackamas County Tax, and do not mail cash.

Online payments run through US Bank at apps.clackamas.us/pay/at. An e-check costs $3, credit cards and MasterCard debit cost 2.49%, and Visa debit costs $3.95. Bank bill pay is handled by your bank, can take several business days and counts only when the county posts it.

Three due dates apply: November 15, February 15 and May 15. A weekend or holiday pushes the date to the next business day. Settle the whole bill by November 15 and you get a 3% discount.

The office does not take prepayment of taxes a district has not certified, except in cases the law allows, such as recording a subdivision or moving a manufactured home. Money is applied to the oldest year first, so a seller who is two years behind cannot target the newer one.

Real property tax is delinquent after May 15, and foreclosure starts once taxes have been late for three years. A statement marks an account facing foreclosure with an asterisk.

Under ORS chapter 312, a foreclosed property is held for two years, and during that period these people can redeem it:

  • anyone who held an interest on the judgment date, and their heirs or devisees
  • anyone with a recorded lien on the property
  • a city or district with a lien on it

To redeem, an owner pays the full judgment with interest, a 5% penalty and a fee. With no redemption, the county receives the deed from the tax collector. Equity above the debt is at stake here, not only the tax bill, which is the strongest reason to sell before a judgment instead of after.

Watch your statement for the asterisk. If you see it, call the office the same week and ask exactly which years are late and what has to be paid to stop the clock.

The Property Value Appeals Board hears appeals, and petitions go to the County Clerk by December 31. Clerk staff at 503-655-8662 can send petition forms, and Assessment and Taxation at 503-655-8671 can talk through the value before you file.

The clerk takes petitions once statements are out. Hearings open on or after the first Monday in February, and the board finishes by March 15.

Measure 5 and Measure 50 limit most bills, so an appeal changes the amount mostly when real market value sits close to assessed value, or when the property was valued with features it does not have. Photos, an appraisal and sales near January 1 give the board something concrete.

First, the tax year. It runs July 1 through June 30 with the lien attaching July 1. Have escrow show how this year gets divided and confirm no older year is owed.

Next, look for a senior or disabled deferral. Qualifying owners have the state pay the county, with a 6% lien recorded against the house. Selling or transferring the home ends the program, and the balance, interest and recording costs come due by August 15 of the next year. Heirs can be on the hook too.

Last, prepare the seller disclosure. ORS 105.464 gives the buyer five days to revoke after getting it. Court-appointed personal representatives and foreclosing financial institutions can claim an exclusion.

sections.h2: Records to collect before you list
sections.html:
Pull the parcel from the county's online records and write down its real market value, its maximum assessed value and the districts that bill it. Check the statement for an asterisk, and ask whether any deferral lien is recorded. These three items tell a buyer's lender and the escrow officer what to expect at the table.

For a Lake Oswego house the questions will differ from those on a Mount Hood cabin, so tell the escrow officer early which kind of property you are selling and whether wells, septic or private roads are involved.

Being behind does not stop a cash sale. The county supplies a payoff figure, the title company deducts it from your proceeds at the table, and the new deed gets recorded. Ask for the payoff broken out by year if more than one is open.

Call Assessment and Taxation before you choose how to sell. Find out how far behind the account is, whether a deferral lien exists, and what the payoff would be on the closing date you want. Then compare a listing, which needs repairs, showings and time, against a written offer that settles everything at the title company.

faqs.q: When are Clackamas County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Bills are due November 15, February 15 and May 15, and the date shifts to the next business day when it falls on a weekend or holiday. Paying in full by November 15 earns a 3% discount.

faqs.q: How do I contact Clackamas County Assessment and Taxation?
faqs.a: Call 503-655-8671 or email propertytaxinfo@clackamas.us. The office is at 150 Beavercreek Road, Room 135, Oregon City, and keeps Monday to Thursday hours from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

faqs.q: Does Clackamas County foreclose on unpaid property taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. Foreclosure begins after taxes have been delinquent for three years, and the owner then has a two-year redemption period after the judgment. Unredeemed property is deeded to the county.

faqs.q: Can I lower my Clackamas County property tax by appealing?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Because taxes follow the lower of market value and assessed value, a lower market value only helps if it drops below assessed value. File with the County Clerk by December 31.

faqs.q: What do I owe if I sell a house with a deferred property tax lien?
faqs.a: You owe the deferred taxes, 6% annual interest and recording costs. The state program makes the balance due by August 15 of the year after a sale or ownership change.
